rule: A tested link is recommended only on checked causal evidence (strong or good, or suggestive when it rests on a single clean trial), and only when the program runs the studied model. A code alone never earns credit: a code says what a program works toward, and the evidence is about specific program models.
associatedRule: A research-associated link rests on consistent correlational evidence: a meta-analysis, or several long-term studies that point the same way and adjust for prior achievement or attendance. A single survey at one point in time does not count. These outcomes are associated with the indicator; the studies do not show that a program building them moves it.
associatedCaution: Programs often attract students who are already more engaged, so an association can overstate what the program itself does.

links.pathway: Tutoring programs that build children's reading skills raise scores on standardized reading tests, and partner-run versions using trained, paid tutors (including national service members) work too, though effects are smaller at scale.
links.modelMatch: Tutoring during the school day by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as AmeriCorps), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured reading curriculum, in kindergarten to grade 3. Volunteer and virtual tutoring count only at the lower sizes below. Homework help or general after-school time does not qualify.
links.conditions: Tutoring during the school day by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as AmeriCorps), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured reading curriculum, in kindergarten to grade 3. Volunteer and virtual tutoring count only at the lower sizes below. Homework help or general after-school time does not qualify.
links.typicalEffect: SPARK (Milwaukee) randomized trial: 0.12 standard deviations on a national reading test. A one-year follow-on trial of the same model: significant gains on two reading tests. Education Corps randomized trial: 0.17 at mid-year. Push-in kindergarten tutoring: oral reading 0.23, district reading level 0.11. Paraeducator tutoring in grade 1: better on 5 of 6 tests. Reading Corps: significant gains in kindergarten to grade 3. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 and small-group reading 0.33 on state tests. Nashville at scale: 0.04 to 0.09. Volunteer tutoring meta-analysis: 0.23. Virtual tutoring: 0.05 to 0.08 (one-to-one 0.07 to 0.12). Meta-analysis of small-group instruction by adults: about 0.35 to 0.45 on mixed measures. Plan on 0.05 to 0.15 on the state test.
links.magnitude: At 0.16 standard deviations, about 6 more participants in 100 reach proficient, assuming participants resemble the District's tested students (base rate about 31 to 33 percent). If the partner tutors 10 percent of a school's tested students, the school rate rises about 0.6 percentage points. Volunteer-trial sizes (0.10 to 0.13) give about 4 to 5 more in 100 participants.
links.caveats: Most effects are on national or researcher tests, not the Pennsylvania test. Philadelphia's Experience Corps volunteer program (2016-17 only) showed no overall difference in kindergarten to grade 3, and the grade 3 comparison group scored slightly higher. Effects shrink as programs scale.

links.pathway: Tutoring programs that build children's math skills raise scores on math tests, but at scale the gain on state tests is small or not detectable.
links.modelMatch: Tutoring by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as Math Corps), during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured math curriculum. Volunteer tutoring and tutoring offered only before or after school do not qualify.
links.conditions: Tutoring by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as Math Corps), during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured math curriculum. Volunteer tutoring and tutoring offered only before or after school do not qualify.
links.typicalEffect: Math Corps randomized trials: 0.17 (0.24 at intended dosage) and about 0.18 on broad math tests; the state test was not significantly different in the grades 4 to 8 and statewide trials. A matched study of another tutoring corps: 0.10. Early-grade protocols: Number Rockets 0.34, Pirate Math 0.37, fractions tutoring 0.51, small-group early math 0.19 (researcher or national tests). Tutoring meta-analysis 0.36. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 on state math. Nashville at scale: no average math effect. Volunteer tutoring: math not significant. Plan on 0 to 0.10 on the state test.
links.magnitude: At 0.16 to 0.21 standard deviations, about 5 to 7 more participants in 100 reach proficient on the grades 3-8 math test (base rate about 25 percent) and about 6 to 8 in 100 in grade 3 (base rate about 34 percent). If the partner tutors 10 percent of a school's tested students, the school rate rises about 0.5 to 0.8 percentage points.
links.caveats: Most gains are on non-state tests; the two Math Corps trials that used the state test found no significant difference.

links.pathway: Daily small-group math tutoring, scheduled as a class period in ninth and tenth grade, raises high school math test scores, including New York's Algebra I end-of-course exam.
links.modelMatch: A tutoring period every school day, built into the school schedule, with paid, trained tutors and groups of two to four students. A version that alternates tutor days with computer practice was tested in one randomized trial. A fully online version rests on one matched comparison only.
links.conditions: A tutoring period every school day, built into the school schedule, with paid, trained tutors and groups of two to four students. A version that alternates tutor days with computer practice was tested in one randomized trial. A fully online version rests on one matched comparison only.
links.typicalEffect: Average 0.14 (three trials: 0.09, 0.14, 0.19); technology-blended version 0.23 for participants at about 30 percent lower cost. Meta-analysis: small-group instruction 0.38, math tests 0.34.
links.magnitude: In the trial, students offered tutoring scored 0.19 standard deviations higher on end-of-year standardized math tests (one cohort; Regents exams in New York, the PSAT in Chicago). In the online version's matched comparison, 8 more students in 100 passed New York's Algebra I exam by the end of ninth grade (39 versus 31 percent). For participants, 0.16 to 0.37 standard deviations would move about 4 to 10 more in 100 to proficient on an exam where about 15.5 percent are proficient, if the effect carried over to the Keystone exam, which no study tested. Tutoring a quarter of a school's Algebra I takers would add about 1 to 2.5 percentage points to the school rate.
links.caveats: Outcomes are district or national tests, not the Keystone exam. Population was mostly entering ninth graders. The online version showed weaker effects for boys and for students who entered high school far behind. New York's Regents passing score is not the Keystone proficiency cut, so these rates do not translate into Keystone rates. The program needs a slot in the school day, so a partner runs it with a school, not on its own.

links.pathway: Universal social and emotional learning curricula taught during the school day raise students' test scores slightly, and the gain is smaller in the largest, most rigorous trials than in earlier reviews.
links.modelMatch: A universal, sequenced social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day by trained teachers or partner staff, for at least a full school year. After-school or pull-out social skills groups and one-off assemblies do not qualify.
links.conditions: A universal, sequenced social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day by trained teachers or partner staff, for at least a full school year. After-school or pull-out social skills groups and one-off assemblies do not qualify.
links.typicalEffect: Meta-analysis of school-based programs: overall 0.08 standard deviations (math 0.08, English 0.07), smaller in randomized trials than in quasi-experiments. Another meta-analysis: reading 0.25 and math 0.26, with smaller effects in large rigorous randomized trials. Positive Action in Chicago: the authors report a marginal math gain, the clearinghouse finds state reading and math not significant, and absenteeism improved. Positive Action in Hawaii: large gains per the authors, not significant in the clearinghouse review. INSIGHTS: early gains faded by middle school. A classroom social skills program: no main effects. Plan on 0.05 to 0.08 on state tests.
links.magnitude: At 0.10 standard deviations, about 3 to 4 more students in 100 reach proficient on the grades 3-8 English language arts or math test. Because the model is whole-class, a school where every class uses the curriculum could see a rise of that order; a partner teaching one grade of six would add about 0.5 to 0.6 percentage points to a school's grades 3-8 rate. Publication bias makes the true figure likely smaller.
links.caveats: The federal seven-program social and emotional learning trial could not use test scores (it used rating scales), so it neither supports nor refutes this link. A science effect (0.06) rests on three estimates and is not added. Program developers ran several of the positive trials.

links.pathway: Students attending more school days is exactly what this indicator counts. This is a definition, not evidence that any program type moves attendance.
links.modelMatch: Any program, provided the partner shows from school records that its participants' share at or above 90 percent of days rose against a comparison group. A program model with a tested attendance effect (personalized absence messages to families, or a community school) gives a reason to expect it; other models need their own data.
links.conditions: Counts only school-day attendance from school records, reported as the share of participants at or above 90 percent of instructional days, against a comparison group. Program-day attendance is a separate output code (Participation, Dosage and Reach, A2.5).
links.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. Program models with tested attendance effects are personalized absence messages to families and community schools.
links.magnitude: Each participant who moves from below to at or above 90 percent of days adds one student to the count: in a school of 500, moving 10 students adds 2 percentage points.
links.caveats: Chronic absence (missing 10 percent or more of days) is close to the complement of this indicator, but District enrollment rules can differ. School asthma education, school health centers and tutoring did not move school-record attendance, so a program type alone is no reason to expect a gain.

links.typicalEffect: Texting trial in 4 urban districts (26,843 students, kindergarten to grade 5): chronic absence 2.4 to 3.6 percentage points lower from 20.5 percent (12 to 18 percent), 3.5 to 7.3 points lower for students with high prior absence, at about 6 to 9 dollars per student. 47 rural districts in 16 states: absences down 1.7 percent for the offer (about 0.2 days) and 4.5 percent for families reached (about half a day), at 4.07 dollars per student. Teacher postcards, preschool to grade 2: absences down 8.3 percent. Teacher-parent outreach in grades 1-2 in five schools: 5 to 6 points fewer students with 4 or more absences. Redesigned truancy notices: 0.07 fewer days absent than the standard notice.
links.magnitude: Plan on about 2 percent fewer absences at scale (1.9 percent across six district-run trials), about 0.3 days for a student with 15 absences, which barely moves the 90-percent share. The best Philadelphia arm cut chronic absence from 36.0 to 31.9 percent among high-risk students who got mailings, about 4 points; if such students were a third of a school, that would be a little over 1 point on the school rate. Treat 1 point as an upper planning figure.
links.caveats: Effects are small per student and smaller at scale. A single nudge letter at the 90-percent line had no overall effect (a middle school subgroup improved). Texts about grades and attendance in grades 6-11 in one Midwest district did not change chronic absence. Partners need record access through the school or district.

links.pathway: Community schools that coordinate health, family and learning services on site cut chronic absence in New York City and California, but not in Tennessee.
links.modelMatch: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained at least three years.
links.conditions: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained at least three years.
links.typicalEffect: New York City: chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 (high school), three-year average. California (matched schools, first full year): chronic absence fell 1.5 points more than in matched schools (about 30 percent more), 2.8 points in elementary schools. Tennessee (statewide, staggered adoption): chronic absence rose 1.3 points (5.9 percent). Plan on the California size, not the New York City size.
links.magnitude: The school is the treated unit. Chronic absence fell 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 points (high school) on a three-year average. Because chronic absence is close to the complement of this indicator, the school's 90-percent share would rise by roughly 7 to 8 points if the New York City result carried over. This is the largest school-level effect in the map, and it is for the whole model, not one partner.
links.caveats: The Tennessee estimate is less certain because of pre-existing trends. Massachusetts Wraparound Zones, a lighter model, showed no attendance effect. Case management in Kalamazoo elementary schools improved attendance (size not checked), unlike the national case-management trial of integrated student supports.

links.pathway: Winning a summer jobs lottery in Boston raised on-time graduation and cut dropout; a Chicago summer jobs trial found no change in school persistence.
links.modelMatch: A paid summer jobs program for high school students, filled by lottery or similar open selection, as in Boston.
links.conditions: A paid summer jobs program for high school students, filled by lottery or similar open selection, as in Boston.
links.typicalEffect: Boston lottery: higher on-time graduation and lower dropout (existing link). Chicago lottery: no significant change in school persistence through the third year after the program, with confidence intervals ruling out more than 4 to 5 more days present.
links.magnitude: Among participants, +4.4 points on on-time graduation. If a partner places 5 percent of a high school's cohort, the school's four-year rate rises about 0.2 points. Dropouts: 2.5 fewer per 100 participants over four years, so a partner serving 200 students would mean about 5 fewer dropouts in the District count. The Chicago and New York City results suggest the expected effect elsewhere is smaller.
links.caveats: One positive city trial and one null on persistence, so suggestive only. The older Summer Training and Education Program trial does not test summer jobs because its control group also had a summer job (dropout 29.2 versus 25.1 and 21.6 versus 22.6 percent, not significant). The dropout part is weaker than the graduation part.

links.pathway: Passing ninth-grade courses and earning credits strongly predicts graduating in four years, including in Philadelphia. Credits are also a graduation requirement by rule.
links.modelMatch: A program serving ninth graders that tracks its own students' course passing and credits from school records (for example through a data-sharing agreement) and acts on them.
links.conditions: Only when a program reports its own students' course passing or credits from school records. Use it as a tracking signal, not as a measured contribution. The dropout part is a separate, not-recommended row.
links.typicalEffect: Philadelphia: 82 percent graduation on track against 56 percent off track (87.8 to 89.2 against 43.3 to 48.8 percent in district cohorts); Chicago: on-track students 3.5 times more likely to graduate.
links.magnitude: No effect size is credited. Philadelphia on-track ninth graders graduated at 82 percent against 56 percent off track; that 26-point gap is a correlation, and program-caused gains are likely far smaller.
links.caveats: Predictive, not causal. No checked study shows that a program-caused rise in course passing raises graduation: the Saga tutoring trial cut course failures but its direct graduation estimate was not significant, and Diplomas Now moved warning flags without moving graduation.

links.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. The program model with a tested graduation effect is paid summer jobs for high school students; attendance gains may also help a little.
links.magnitude: Each participant in the cohort who graduates on time instead of later or not at all adds one student to the count: in a cohort of 400, 4 more on-time graduates add 1 percentage point.

associated.pathway: Regular participation in 21st Century Community Learning Centers after-school programs (30 or more days a year) is associated with slightly fewer school-day absences than matched non-participants with similar prior-year attendance. Randomized trials have not shown that the programs cause this.
associated.basis: Matched comparisons that adjust for prior-year attendance in independent state samples (Texas statewide, New Jersey) and in Philadelphia point the same way; randomized trials of after-school programs found no attendance effect.
associated.typicalEffect: Texas statewide: regular participants attended 0.3 to 1.4 percentage points more school days than matched non-participants (about 0.5 to 3.4 days a year, more at higher participation); two years at 60 or more days a year added about 1.1 to 1.2 points. New Jersey 2022-23: unexcused absence rate about 0.4 points lower (about three quarters of a day) than students who attended 15 days or fewer. Washington 2012-13: 14 percent (30 or more days) and 33 percent (60 or more days) fewer unexcused absences. Texas site-level study (779 centers): median center effect 0.14 standard deviations, with wide spread. Philadelphia (11 grantees): elementary regular participants were less likely to have 10 or more unexcused absences; no difference in middle or high school. Gains this size move the 90-percent share only for students close to the line.
associated.caveats: Students who keep coming differ from those who do not, and matching on prior attendance handles this only in part. A meta-analysis of controlled studies of after-school programs for at-risk youth found a small, non-significant attendance effect, and randomized trials of middle school after-school programs and of After School Matters in Chicago found no attendance difference. Most state reports come from one evaluator (American Institutes for Research); the Texas site-level and Philadelphia studies are by other evaluators. New Jersey's 2022-23 comparison group is low-attending participants, not non-participants. Two arts-focused Philadelphia centers found no attendance difference. Test-score effects are near zero.

associated.pathway: Playing on a school sports team is associated with fewer absences during the season, comparing each student with themselves.

associated.pathway: Homelessness and eviction are associated with more school absences, and eviction itself causes more absences and school changes.
associated.basis: Two independent studies: one follows students and adjusts for prior attendance, the other uses random assignment of eviction cases to judges.
associated.typicalEffect: Los Angeles (weighting on grade 3 attendance and math): homeless students missed 5.8 more days. associated.caveats: Programs that rehoused families did not raise attendance. The eviction study found little effect on grade 3 to 8 test scores, so no link to the grade 3 reading test is claimed and S5 is dropped from this row.

associated.pathway: Academic self-concept (how capable students believe they are in school subjects) is associated with slightly higher later test scores, compared with students who started at the same achievement level.
associated.basis: Two meta-analyses of long-term studies, each adjusting for earlier achievement, plus a five-year study of 3,425 students.
associated.typicalEffect: A small path of about 0.08 from self-concept to later achievement, net of earlier achievement, in both meta-analyses. The path from achievement to later self-concept is about twice as large (0.16).
associated.caveats: Holds for academic self-concept, not for growth mindset or general self-esteem (Self-Worth, Y5.4), where national long-term studies found no association once earlier achievement is counted. For self-efficacy, a meta-analysis found that in children only earlier performance predicts later self-efficacy, not the reverse. A 2024 reanalysis argues that adjusting for an earlier score can produce spurious effects of this kind.

associated.pathway: Failing courses and low grades in the middle grades or ninth grade are associated with later dropping out, beyond what eighth-grade test scores and background predict.
associated.basis: Long-term cohort studies in Philadelphia, Chicago and Baltimore, two of which compare against eighth-grade test scores or pre-high-school characteristics.
associated.typicalEffect: In Philadelphia, sixth graders who failed math were 54 percent less likely to graduate, and those who failed English 42 percent less likely. In Chicago, freshman grades and course failures explained about 39 percent of the variation in graduation, against about 12 percent for test scores and background.
associated.caveats: These are early-warning predictions, not effects of raising grades. Most studies count students who did not graduate rather than the District's dropout count. The Philadelphia cohorts are from the 1990s and 2000s.

associated.pathway: Attention, task persistence and impulse control at school entry are associated with higher later reading and math scores, beyond children's early academic skills.
associated.basis: An analysis of six long-term datasets with a meta-analysis, replicated in two Canadian cohorts, plus two further long-term studies that adjust for earlier achievement.
associated.typicalEffect: Effects are small. Early math skills predicted later scores most, then reading, then attention. In a national study, kindergarten executive functions predicted grade 2 scores by about 0.05 to 0.12 of a standard deviation after earlier achievement.
associated.caveats: Holds for young children only: in two middle-school studies, self-control did not predict changes in test scores once earlier scores were counted (it did predict report-card grades). Academic Perseverance (Y1.10) fits early task persistence; Emotion Regulation and Coping (Y4.2) fits only its impulse-control part. Social skills and prosocial behavior were not associated with later scores in the same studies.

associated.pathway: High schools where students report better relationships with teachers are associated with fewer students dropping out, after accounting for tenth-grade math scores and background.
associated.basis: Two separate national long-term studies (3,840 students in 190 schools; 7,779 students in 431 schools), both adjusting for tenth-grade math achievement.
associated.typicalEffect: In one study, a school one standard deviation higher on student-teacher relations had about 86 percent lower odds of a student dropping out, but only in schools under 1,500 students. In the other, a better relationship climate went with lower dropout by senior year.
associated.caveats: This is about a whole school's relationship climate, not one student's mentor or relationship. In the first study the association disappeared in schools over 1,500 students, which matters for large Philadelphia high schools. Both studies count dropping out by senior year, not the four-year graduation rate. A meta-analysis of unadjusted associations found only a non-significant trend for poor teacher relationships and dropout. The same studies found no association with test-score gains.

associated.pathway: Students who do their homework, take part and pay attention in class are associated with lower dropout, compared with students at the same achievement level.
associated.basis: Two separate long-term studies (1,272 Maryland youth followed from grade 7; a national sample of high school students), both with achievement in the model.
associated.typicalEffect: In the national sample, teacher-rated academic engagement (standardized coefficient about -0.27) and student-reported behavioral engagement (about -0.30) each predicted lower dropout by grade 12, with test achievement (about -0.20) in the same model.
associated.caveats: Narrow: two studies. In the national sample, achievement was measured at the same time as engagement, not before it, and behavioral engagement includes skipping and lateness, which overlaps attendance.
